title: Durga's Promise Before the Battle
story:
The night before the great battle, when the two armies lay camped on the plain of Kurukshetra, Krishna gave Arjuna an order that sounded more like a ritual than a plan for war. "Cleanse yourself, mighty-armed one," he said, "and on the eve of this battle recite your hymn to Durga, so that the defeat of your enemies may be assured."

At dawn the five Pandava brothers and their allies would meet the army of their cousins, the Kauravas, on this same field. Years of insult and exile and a rigged game of dice had pushed the two families to this plain, and now nothing was left but the war itself. Yet on the last night, the first command from Arjuna's charioteer — Krishna, who would drive his chariot in the morning — was not about formations or weapons. It was about a hymn.

Arjuna did not ask why. He stepped down from the chariot and, in the quiet of the camp, with his palms joined, recited the hymn exactly as he had been taught. He praised the goddess Durga under her many names, and every name told what she was: Kali of the dark and tawny hue; Mahakali, who brings good to her worshippers; the giver of victory, who carries a banner of peacock plumes and holds spear, sword, and shield; she who slew the demon Kaitabha; the mother of Skanda, the war-god; the younger sister of the chief of cowherds, born in the house of Nanda — the cowherd chief who had raised Krishna. He named her the twilight and the day, the sleep of all creatures and their beauty, the strength that makes the sun and moon shine; he called her the wisdom of the Vedas, the oldest sacred songs, and the power that haunts wild and dangerous places and the homes of her worshippers, always defeating the demons. And with his inner self cleansed, he prayed: "Let victory always attend me through your grace on the field of battle."

Perhaps that prayer was what was heard. Durga, who is always gracious to the world, understood the depth of Arjuna's devotion, and she appeared in the sky above the camp, in the very presence of Krishna. "Within a short time you shall conquer your enemies, O Pandava," the goddess said. "You cannot be defeated — for you have Narayana, the Lord whom men call Krishna, to aid you again. Not even Indra, the king of the gods who hurls the thunderbolt, could overcome you."

Having said this, the goddess who grants boons vanished as suddenly as she had come. Arjuna stood a moment with the promise in his heart, then mounted his chariot. And Krishna and Arjuna, seated together on that great car, blew their celestial conches, and the sound rolled out over the sleeping armies like the first note of the war that would begin at dawn.

Sanjaya, telling all this to Dhritarashtra, the blind king of the Kurus, added that a man who recites this hymn at dawn need fear nothing — not the spirits of the dark, not snakes or creatures of fang and tooth, not even angry kings. He is victorious in every dispute, freed from every bond, and lives a hundred years in health and strength. But the Kauravas, Sanjaya said, were caught in the net of death and did not know that the two who stood on that one chariot were Nara and Narayana — the ancient seer-pair whose forms, the bards said, Arjuna and Krishna had taken — nor that the hour of their kingdom had already arrived. The sage Vyasa, whom some call Dwaipayana, the wandering sage Narada, the seer Kanwa, and the blameless Rama — Balarama, Krishna's own brother — had all tried to turn Dhritarashtra's son from his course, and he would not hear them. Where righteousness is, there victory is.
reflection: Krishna's first preparation for the war is an act of worship, not a tactic: before Arjuna is taught to fight, he is sent to bow. And the goddess's promise — that the invincible one has Narayana to aid him — names what the hymn has accomplished: the charioteer and the goddess are already on Arjuna's side, and the battle is blessed before a single arrow is loosed.
next_story_tease: At dawn, Krishna would drive the chariot between the two armies.
hero_scene: Durga appears in the night sky above the camp on the eve of battle, radiant and gracious, blessing Arjuna who stands with joined hands beside his chariot while Krishna watches from the car.
